notes.key_messages: • Candidates should go through their plans when answering Question 3 before writing their response. There is no need to list apparatus or variables at the start of the plan. • When a question asks for the name of a chemical, a correct formula is always acceptable. However, if a candidate answers with an incorrect formula, then the mark will not be awarded. • Candidates should be aware that the mark allocation reflects the number of valid points to be made for parts of questions.
notes.general_comments: Most candidates successfully completed all questions and there was no evidence that candidates were short of time. The complete range of marks was seen. The paper discriminated successfully between candidates of different abilities but was accessible to all. The majority of candidates were able to complete tables of results from readings on diagrams and then handle the data obtained as in Question 2.
notes.1a: Most candidates correctly completed the tables of results. Many did not seem to understand what was required for ‘temperature change since the start’ and gave temperature changes from the previous reading. A number of candidates produced random numbers.
notes.1b: The y-axis often had an incorrect scale and temperatures were plotted instead of temperature changes. Curves were often not smooth, and labels were missing.
notes.1c: This was generally well answered. A small number misjudged where 13cm would be and read off the value for Experiment 2 instead of Experiment 1.
notes.1d: Few candidates could explain that this was because the acid was in excess. ‘Reaction had finished’ was creditworthy. Vague references to solutions being used up were frequently seen.
notes.1e: Many candidates did not deduce that solution G was more concentrated. The idea of changing concentrations was common.
notes.1f: This was well answered. Most candidates knew that the polystyrene cup would be an insulator. A common misconception was that the polystyrene cup would react with the acid or melt.
notes.1g: Vague answers referred to a burette being hard to use or not big enough.
notes.2a: Many candidates gained credit for effervescence but did not do the limewater test.
notes.2b: The majority of candidates identified a red coloured flame correctly.
notes.2c: Many candidates identified solid I as lithium carbonate.
notes.2d: Many candidates reported the formation of a white precipitate. A significant number stated that the precipitate would be cream-yellow or white-cream and was insoluble.
notes.2e: Candidates noted that the precipitate was insoluble.
notes.2f: Many candidates incorrectly described a change.
notes.2g: A white precipitate was often given.
notes.2h: Solid J was often identified as calcium chloride.
